normative_action: When SPECIFICATION.md is non-empty it is authoritative for project-specific functional requirements and observable product behaviour; an empty template file is intentional.

Do not silently weaken, contradict or materially extend approved behaviour; do not invent user-visible behaviour, limits, defaults, restrictions or workflows, also not merely because the specification does not forbid them.
If an omitted detail must be decided and materially affects observable behaviour, propose the smallest reasonable option and ask for approval.
Routine internal implementation choices that do not change observable behaviour do not require approval.

Observable string semantics (case, collation, culture/ordinal, normalization, trimming, uniqueness, lookup) are product behaviour; when undefined and material do not choose silently, ask for approval.

SPECIFICATION.md and CUSTOM_SETTINGS.md must not contradict; on conflict stop and resolve which source must be corrected.

Synchronize every surface affected by an approved tunable value (custom-settings).
Never store secrets, environment-specific connection details, package versions, HTTP status codes, ports, migration identifiers or incidental constants in CUSTOM_SETTINGS.md.
Classify every consequential choice as Decided, Delegated or Reserved.
Decided choices (instruction system, product inputs, recorded decisions, choices required by the specification or established structure) are followed and not reopened without approval.
Delegated choices (local, reversible, no boundary/dependency/convention/contract/behaviour change) are decided without asking approval.
Reserved choices require explicit approval before implementation; the list is a minimum ('at least').

Changing the project reference graph is Reserved.

normative_action: Never hardcode or commit real secrets, credentials, private keys, tokens or production connection strings, including in example configuration.
Local secret mechanism for development; environment-specific injection or managed secret store for deployments; do not assume an unchosen cloud provider.
Treat data crossing the trusted boundary (requests, uploads, external responses, messages, user identifiers/filters) as untrusted and validate it at the owning layer when assumptions matter.
Do not trust client-provided file metadata such as MIME type as authoritative when handling or security decisions depend on content.
Use parameterized database access; never concatenate untrusted input into SQL.
Enforce authorization on the server; route guards, hidden buttons and client checks are UX, not a security boundary.
Anonymous access is deliberate and visible; avoid redundant authorization markers when a secure global/fallback policy expresses intent.
Do not implement custom token/password security, hashing or reset-token cryptography when platform authentication/identity facilities cover the requirement.
For Bearer/OIDC validate what the issuer requires (issuer, audience, signing authority, lifetime); never disable validation to make a token work.
Do not expose authentication-failure detail revealing secrets or account state; avoid account-enumeration leaks.
With automatic browser cookie credentials include CSRF protection; a single-page frontend does not remove the risk.
Do not claim one browser token-storage mechanism is universally secure; choose by threat model; never log tokens.
Production traffic with credentials/sensitive data uses TLS respecting hosting topology; never disable certificate validation.
No custom cryptography when a well-reviewed platform mechanism is appropriate.
CORS is the narrowest policy satisfying actual browser clients; never credentialed requests with unrestricted origins.
Security-sensitive authorization/permission/required-control checks fail safely; do not convert lookup/configuration failures into success.
Prefer visible startup/configuration failure over insecure fallback when a required security control cannot be configured.
Do not expose stack traces, SQL details, connection strings, internal paths, secrets or sensitive exception details in public API errors.
Do not expose secrets, credentials, connection details, stack traces or unnecessary diagnostics through publicly reachable health responses.

Never log passwords, tokens, private keys, auth secrets or full payment credentials; avoid personal data without a permitted operational need, prefer stable technical identifiers; lower log levels do not make data safe.
Do not serialize arbitrary request bodies, domain objects or sensitive payloads into logs by default; log minimal non-sensitive context.
Log an unexpected exception once at the handling boundary, not in every layer.
Add a dependency only for a concrete current requirement of the change; 'approved' or 'conditional' does not mean install by default.
Keep each dependency in the narrowest project or workspace that requires it.
Remove a dependency the current change makes unused when safe to verify.
why_extra_or_uncertain: Removal obligation not in the oracle.

normative_action: Do not perform unrelated dependency cleanup during a narrowly scoped task.
Prefer clear correct code first; no specialized optimizations without a concrete reason; prefer measurement for non-trivial optimization.
Advanced techniques (precompiled queries, specialized async return types, pooling, custom serialization, aggressive caching, raw SQL for performance) only for a measured or demonstrated need.
Filter/project in the database, avoid round trips, over-fetching and N+1, paginate large result sets.
Caching is not a default requirement; introduce only for a clear need; choose implementation by deployment, consistency and staleness.
Cache keys uniquely represent the value with all user/tenant/context dimensions; no global keys for user/tenant data.
Invalidate/update cache only consistently with successful mutations; the cache is never a second source of truth.
Every cache entry has a lifetime or another explicit invalidation strategy.
External I/O has bounded execution time; avoid overlapping unclear timeout mechanisms.
Retry only when repetition is safe; never automatically retry state-changing operations without idempotency or another duplicate-safety mechanism.
Respect Retry-After or equivalent guidance where appropriate; never retry indefinitely or aggressively.
Use a fallback only when its result is semantically acceptable; never hide correctness failures behind defaults.
Caller cancellation is not a transient failure; do not classify or retry it as one.
Normal client cancellation is not a server failure; do not map it to 500 or log it as an unhandled failure.
Health checks stay cheap and deterministic; no business workflows or expensive/mutating database work.
Liveness avoids external dependencies that could cause restart loops (default); readiness may depend on required capabilities and reflects startup/dependency availability.

Choose the narrowest test level that meaningfully verifies behaviour; integration tests when wiring, HTTP, persistence, serialization, authentication or component interaction is the subject; no fixed ratio.
Tests verify observable behaviour, not private methods, call sequences, implementation classes or the algorithm; interaction verification only when the interaction is the specified behaviour.
Test against the actual provider when provider behaviour matters; never claim provider fidelity from a different provider.
Tests are deterministic, order-independent and isolated from Production/Development data, uncontrolled external systems and shared mutable state.
Tests start from a known state and own their setup; never depend on development seeding or other tests.
For small finite input spaces prefer explicit declarative cases; state expected results instead of computing them.
Descriptive test names (scenario/condition and expected behaviour, e.g. MethodOrScenario_Condition_ExpectedBehavior); follow an established project convention.
Do not generate low-value tests merely to increase coverage; coverage is diagnostic, not a target.

Dependencies point inward: Domain none; Application→Domain; Infrastructure→Application, Domain; Api→Application and Infrastructure only for composition/registration; inner layers never depend on outer layers or Infrastructure-specific types.
If a feature seems to need an outward reference reconsider the abstraction boundary instead of adding it.
Domain stays independent of persistence/web/transport frameworks, HTTP, persistence and external-service concerns.
Simple domain entities by default; use-case and workflow rules in Application Services; validation rules, immutable fields, transitions or edit rules do not justify a Rich Domain Model.
Move behaviour into Domain only for non-trivial invariants benefiting from encapsulation; otherwise Rich Domain/DDD tactical patterns require approval unless the approved specification requires them.
Do not add factories, private setters, transition methods, Aggregate Roots, Domain Events, Specifications, Domain Services, systematic Value Objects or similar merely to look domain-driven.
Application Services are the default use-case orchestration; a large service is a signal to reconsider responsibilities, not to adopt another pattern.
Define persistence/external-service abstractions in Application when needed; keep infrastructure details out.
Application must not depend on persistence-framework types/APIs, provider-specific types or web transport types.
Infrastructure translates remote HTTP responses into Application abstractions; do not leak HttpResponseMessage or transport concerns into Application.
Keep cache technology out of Domain; no infrastructure cache APIs in Application without a deliberate boundary abstraction.
Program.cs in Api is the composition root and may register Infrastructure implementations.
Registration close to the owning layer: Application services by Application, persistence/adapters by Infrastructure, Api the composition root.
Constructor injection for required dependencies; avoid service-locator and property injection.
Never capture a shorter-lived dependency inside a longer-lived service.
The persistence framework is an Infrastructure detail: use it normally there but do not leak its concepts into Application.
Do not cripple repository implementations to preserve a generic abstraction; the boundary hides persistence from Application, not the framework from Infrastructure.
Repository interfaces are inward-facing contracts defined in Application and implemented in Infrastructure.
Prefer specific cohesive repository interfaces over table-mirroring generic CRUD contracts; approved Aggregate Roots are natural boundaries.
Repository interfaces expose no IQueryable, framework context/set/expression or provider types; return materialized results.
Application must not depend on IGenericRepository<T> or generic CRUD contracts; a generic base may exist only in Infrastructure to remove real duplication.
IUnitOfWork is the normal commit boundary; repositories stage changes and Application Services commit.
Repositories in one use case share the scoped Unit of Work and context; repositories are injected explicitly; IUnitOfWork is no repository container or service locator.
No explicit transaction APIs until a concrete use case needs more than the normal single save/commit.
Physical structure follows actual responsibilities; no speculative projects, infrastructure, empty trees or generic Common/Helpers/Utils buckets.
Name supporting types so their architectural role is clear from the name and/or directory; split a feature into subdirectories only when a flat directory becomes hard to navigate.
why_extra_or_uncertain: Type-role naming heuristic not in the oracle.

normative_action: Backend test projects receive no broader production references than their scope requires and follow the inward dependency discipline.
HTTP entry points are thin: bind/validate input, invoke Application services, translate outcomes to HTTP responses.
Entry points contain no business logic, persistence-context or concrete-repository access, or manual infrastructure construction.
HTTP status codes and transport semantics belong to Api; Application/Domain return no web result types or status codes.
Do not duplicate equivalent DTOs across Api and Application merely for layer-shaped types; add transport contracts for a concrete boundary benefit.
HTTP failures use a structured problem-details contract whose machine-readable parts stay stable and safe.
Choose 200/201/202/204 by actual semantics; not 200 for everything, 201 for an internal insert, or 202 for completed work.
A successful zero-match collection query returns 200 with an empty collection, not 404.
401 for missing/failed authentication, 403 for not permitted; 404 hiding requires a deliberate consistent policy.
409 for valid requests conflicting with current state; 412 when an explicit precondition such as If-Match fails.
Do not introduce API versioning merely because an API exists; add it for a concrete compatibility need.
Once a version is relied on externally avoid silent breaking changes; a breaking change requires a new version or an approved compatibility strategy.
Use one versioning strategy consistently; URL-segment versioning by default unless requirements justify another.
Do not create separate Domain/persistence models per API version; isolate version-specific transport contracts at the Api boundary.
Deprecating or removing a published API version follows architecture-decision.
API documentation metadata describes the API that actually runs (routes, important statuses, schemas, authentication); no speculative responses.
Represent common expected outcomes explicitly when useful (null, bool, typed outcome, deliberately adopted Result) using the simplest contract.
Do not force a generic Result<T>; no HTTP-named outcome categories in Application; describe Application semantics and map them to HTTP in Api.
No custom business exceptions as the default architecture; no throw/catch to jump between expected branches.
Unexpected failures propagate to centralized boundary handling; avoid repetitive catch/log/rethrow blocks.
Catch only to recover, translate, perform a defined fallback, add context preserving the original, or clean up; do not swallow failures to continue.
Validate each concern at its owning layer: Api transport/contract, Application use-case/workflow rules, Domain non-trivial invariants, Infrastructure external assumptions.
Do not duplicate the same rule at every layer or move Domain invariants into request validators because a library is available.
Organize primarily by feature; avoid application-wide technical buckets and empty folders; keep feature code in its feature and core/shared small.
Route-level lazy loading for meaningful features, not every tiny component.
Pages/components focus on presentation and UI orchestration; do not move trivial presentation logic into services to shrink components.
Backend communication in explicit data-access services; no HTTP calls scattered in components; never import backend Domain types; use frontend API models matching the contract.
Prefer simple local/component/service state before a state-management library.
Follow the documented API error contract; centralize problem-details parsing when practical; never infer behaviour from human-readable messages.
Frontend validation improves UX but never replaces backend validation, data-integrity or security enforcement.
Follow existing conventions and .editorconfig; modern C# when it improves clarity; no mechanical modernization of working code.
No style-only rewrites outside the requested change unless asked; avoid mixing large formatting/modernization with functional work.
New code: file-scoped namespaces when consistent, one primary top-level type per matching file, Async suffix for Task/ValueTask methods unless a contract makes it inappropriate.
Use async APIs for asynchronous I/O; never block with .Result, .Wait() or similar.
Propagate CancellationToken when cancellation is meaningful; no cancellation parameters on purely synchronous code without a use case.
Use TimeProvider for clock-dependent logic needing deterministic tests; do not mechanically replace explicit/stored timestamps.
Never create and dispose an HttpClient per request; use IHttpClientFactory or another long-lived strategy.
Prefer strongly typed options and validate at startup when invalid values prevent correct/secure operation; avoid scattered string IConfiguration lookups.
Api entry points are ASP.NET Core Controllers; do not create Minimal API endpoint groups unless explicitly requested.
IActionResult, ActionResult<T>, ProblemDetails, HttpContext, ClaimsPrincipal, IHttpContextAccessor and StatusCodes stay in Api and never appear in Application or Domain contracts.
ProblemDetails for non-validation failures and ValidationProblemDetails for request validation; stable safe machine-readable fields.

normative_action: PUT may return 201 when it creates a resource at a previously non-existing URI.
202 fits long-running operations, background jobs, asynchronous imports and queued processing.
Return an operation identifier or Location for 202 when practical.
204 fits a successful DELETE or an update whose representation adds no value; never with a body.
For an empty collection 200 with [] beats 204, preserving the representation.
304 only for conditional requests with a still-valid cached representation, not a business 'nothing changed'.
400 for malformed JSON, invalid shape, binding failures and missing transport input, not for authentication failure.
406 when no acceptable representation can be produced; 415 for an unsupported request media type.
422 for structurally valid but semantically invalid requests, or 400 for both when the project deliberately uses it; follow the established convention.
428 when a contract-required precondition (e.g. If-Match) is absent.
429 with Retry-After when known for rate-limited requests; never for validation failures.
500 for unexpected internal failures via centralized handling and ProblemDetails.
502/504 only when acting as an intermediary (invalid upstream response / upstream timeout); do not convert every dependency failure to 502.
503 with Retry-After when meaningful for temporary inability (maintenance, required dependency down, chosen overload semantics).
401 means missing, invalid or expired authentication; 403 cannot be fixed by resending the same credentials.
Distinguish client cancellation, own timeout and upstream timeout before choosing a response; not every TaskCanceledException is a 504.
409 for uniqueness duplicates, incompatible state transitions, conflicting concurrent operations and reused idempotency keys; never for malformed syntax.
Do not claim idempotency merely because duplicates are unlikely.
When a repeated POST must not duplicate effects consider an Idempotency-Key associated with request and result; a reused key with a materially different payload returns 409.

Determine real responses from the whole pipeline; document 201 only when it is the runtime contract and never 204 for an endpoint returning a body; describe ProblemDetails contracts where useful.

Every artifact starts with the one-line header (Level · Owns · Scope · Loads · Depends on); every rule file declares paths.
Update INSTRUCTION_MAP.md for every added, moved or removed artifact.
Run check-instructions.mjs and fix every reported error; keep the always-loaded surface compact.
